Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 15 periods = 600 minutes
Total: 15 periods · 10h 0min

repairs.reason: register backfill (founder ruling 2026-08-02; testing.md C3 / ARV-D-011..013, ARV-D-026)

edits.note: 'Students think quietly, then share in pairs first' keeps the two-stage shape the band is built on

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the word 'vocation' on the board and asks students what they think it means. Students share briefly; teacher does not confirm yet, building curiosity.
Teacher reads the whole poem aloud expressively, stanza by stanza, pointing to the three workers in turn. Students listen with books open to Textbook pp.105–107.
Teacher re-reads each stanza and students echo-read in unison. Teacher pauses after each stanza to ask: 'Who is this worker? What time of day is it?' Students respond orally.
Teacher asks students to close their books and name the three workers the speaker wishes to be. Students call out answers; teacher lists them on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the poem's first encounter, so the read-aloud should be unhurried and expressive — lingering on 'Bangles, crystal bangles!' and the atmospheric simile of the street-lamp. Students at Grade V may not know the word 'vocation'; hold the explanation until the echo-read surfaces enough context from the poem itself.

time_bands.activity: Teacher leads a full choral reading of the poem, all three stanzas together. Students read aloud from Textbook pp.105–107 while teacher models pace and expression.
Teacher reads stanza one again slowly. Students notice: What time is it? Where is the speaker going? What is the hawker doing? Students respond in short spoken phrases.

Stanzas two and three receive the same close observation: students name details — the spade, the dusty clothes, the dark lane, the street-lamp simile. Teacher records key details on the board as students offer them.
Students do a final paired choral reading — partners take alternate stanzas. Teacher circulates, listening for fluency and correct stress.

periods.teacher_notes: Having heard the poem read aloud already, students are ready to voice it themselves. Encourage confident volume — the refrain 'I wish I were …' benefits from being spoken with feeling. Students who notice the street-lamp simile ('a giant with one red eye') are worth pausing on; it is the poem's most vivid image.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — A. (p.108): answer questions 1, 2, and 3 orally in class.

time_bands.activity: Quick paired re-read of stanza one. Partners help each other with any unfamiliar words before the discussion begins.

Let us Think — A. (p.108): Teacher poses question 1 — 'Who is the speaker in the poem?' — and question 2 — 'Why does the speaker want to be a hawker?' Students respond; teacher builds on their answers, pointing back to the poem's lines.
Let us Think — A. (p.108): Teacher poses question 3 — 'What does he like about the gardener?' Students find evidence in stanza two and share in complete spoken sentences.
Students write answers to questions 1–3 in their notebooks individually. Teacher circulates and checks for complete sentences.

periods.teacher_notes: A common pitfall here is students giving one-word answers; prompt them to use evidence from the poem: 'Can you point to the line that tells you?' Questions 1–3 each anchor to a specific stanza, so keeping the textbook open throughout is essential.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — A. (p.108): answer questions 4 and 5 — simile and daily schedule.

time_bands.activity: Teacher re-reads stanza three aloud while students follow. Focus is on the street-lamp simile; teacher asks students to visualise a 'giant with one red eye' before discussing question 4.
Let us Think — A. (p.108): Class discusses question 4 — 'What does the speaker compare the street lamp to?' Teacher draws out the simile, explaining what makes it vivid.

Let us Think — A. (p.108): Question 5 — 'Share the daily schedule of the speaker.' Students look back through all three stanzas to piece together morning, afternoon, and evening events. Pairs draft the schedule together before sharing with the class.
Students write neat answers to questions 4 and 5 in their notebooks. Teacher checks that question 5 responses mention all three time points from the poem.

periods.teacher_notes: Question 5 is the most demanding of the set — it asks students to synthesise across all three stanzas rather than look at one. Students may need a gentle nudge to notice the three time markers: ten in the morning, four in the afternoon, and dusk. The simile in question 4 is worth spending time on, as vivid imagery of this kind is characteristic of Tagore's writing.

periods.activity_title: Think and Discuss — Admiring Other Vocations

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — B. (p.108): discuss why the speaker admires different vocations.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recaps the poem's three workers — hawker, gardener, watchman — by naming them on the board. Students recall one freedom each worker enjoys, speaking in turns.

Let us Think — B. (p.108): Teacher poses question 1 — 'Why does the speaker admire people with different vocations?' Small groups of three discuss, then each group's spokesperson shares the group's view with the class.

Let us Think — B. (p.108): Teacher poses question 2 — 'What are the things that you observe on your way to school and back?' Students describe their own routes, naming workers, sounds, or sights they notice. Teacher encourages full sentences and connects their observations to the poem's speaker.

Quick whole-class share: one student names something they observed on the way to school that could inspire a poem. Teacher affirms the connection to Tagore's method of writing from everyday observation.

periods.teacher_notes: The two discussion questions move from text-bound reasoning to personal observation — a productive widening. Students who conflate admiration with envy may need a gentle prompt: the speaker admires the workers' apparent freedom, not their poverty or lack of education. Keeping the poem open during discussion helps students ground their answers.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen (pp.111–112): groups create WH-questions on the poem and quiz each other.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the WH-question words on the board — who, what, where, when, why, how — and elicits one example question about the poem for each word.

Let us Listen (pp.111–112): Students form groups of five. Each group reads the poem together and writes two WH-questions in their notebooks. Teacher circulates and ensures questions are grounded in the poem's text.
Groups place textbooks in bags. Each group in turn reads their questions aloud; other groups try to answer from memory. Teacher moderates, affirming correct answers and redirecting when needed.

Teacher leads a brief whole-class reflection: which questions were hardest to answer from memory, and why? Students note that the poem's imagery — the simile, the refrain — is memorable even without the book.

periods.teacher_notes: The activity deliberately removes the book during the answering phase, testing how well students have internalised the poem. Expect livelier questions about the street-lamp simile and the watchman; questions about the gardener's stanza are sometimes thinner — prompt groups to include one question about that stanza. Affirm questions that go beyond recall to ask 'why' or 'how'.

periods.activity_title: Personal Share — Wanting to Do Many Things

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak — B. (p.113): share personal experience of wanting to do many things at once.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud the poem's refrain from each stanza — 'I wish I were a hawker … I wish I were a gardener … I wish I were a watchman' — and asks: what do all three wishes have in common? Students identify the theme of wanting freedom from constraints.

Let us Speak — B. (p.113): Teacher models a short personal anecdote — a time she wanted to do many things but could not — naming what she wanted to do and how she felt. This gives students a clear template.
Let us Speak — B. (p.113): Students think quietly, then share in pairs first — what they wanted to do, what stopped them, how it felt. Each pair then nominates one speaker to share with the class.

Teacher draws the sharing to a close by connecting students' experiences back to the poem: the speaker felt exactly this way every morning, afternoon, and evening. Brief class discussion on whether the speaker's feelings are relatable.

periods.teacher_notes: This task invites personal narrative — a rich oracy opportunity, but students sometimes struggle to distinguish between 'many things at once' and 'one forbidden thing'. The poem's speaker exemplifies the feeling of wanting several freedoms simultaneously, which can anchor the discussion. Students who are shy about sharing may find paired sharing easier than whole-class.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — A. (p.109): match poem words to their meanings.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the five words on the board — gong, spade, lane, giant, lantern — and reads each aloud. Students find each word in the poem and read the surrounding line to get context before attempting meanings.
Let us Learn — A. (p.109): Students attempt the matching task individually in their notebooks, writing each word and its meaning. Teacher circulates and notices common uncertainties.

Whole-class check: teacher takes each word in turn, asks a student to read their matched meaning, and the class confirms or corrects. Teacher draws attention to any contextual clues in the poem that helped.

Students use each of the five words in a new sentence of their own (different from the poem's context). Two or three students read their sentences aloud; class evaluates whether the word is used correctly.

periods.teacher_notes: Students commonly confuse 'lane' (a narrow path) with 'road'; pointing to the poem's line about 'no road he must take' alongside 'our lane' helps clarify the distinction. The word 'giant' in the street-lamp simile is metaphorical, so students may need prompting that the definition given is the literal meaning the poet is drawing on for effect.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak — A. (pp.111–112): listen and repeat '-tion'/'-sion' words including 'vocation'.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the eight words on the board — cushion, ration, fashion, tension, mention, attention, nation, vocation — and reads them aloud with exaggerated clarity. Students repeat chorally after each word.

Let us Speak — A. (pp.111–112): Teacher drills pairs of words — ration / nation, mention / attention, fashion / vocation — asking students to listen for the shared ending sound. Students repeat in pairs, then individually. Teacher corrects stress errors (e.g. vo-CA-tion).

Students sort the eight words into two columns on a slip of paper: '-tion' endings and '-sion' endings. Class compares results; teacher confirms that 'cushion' and 'fashion' share a '-shun' sound spelled '-sion'/'-ion'. Brief discussion of why 'vocation' is the chapter's title word.
Quick game: teacher says a word from the list at random; students must repeat it correctly and use it in a phrase. Students who finish early suggest another word they know with the same ending.

periods.teacher_notes: The key phonics point is that both '-tion' and '-sion' are typically pronounced /ʃən/ at this stage, so students need to hear the pattern clearly before they can generalise it. 'Vocation' is the title word and connects the phonics drill to the chapter's theme — worth noting for students. Avoid rushing the individual repetition; auditory accuracy matters more here than speed.
materials: Slips of paper for sorting activity

periods.activity_title: Grammar in Context — Finding and Fixing Errors

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — B. (pp.109–110): underline errors and rewrite correct sentences (sentences 1–5).

homework.task_brief: Let us Learn — B. (pp.109–110): complete sentences 6–10 at home, underlining errors and rewriting.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes two sample sentences on the board — one correct, one with a subject-verb agreement error — and asks students to identify which is wrong and why. This activates awareness of the error types in the task.

Let us Learn — B. (pp.109–110): Students work independently on sentences 1–5, underlining the error in each and writing the corrected sentence in their notebooks. Teacher circulates, noting common error patterns without correcting yet.

Class review: teacher takes each of the five sentences in turn, asks a student to name the error type (subject-verb agreement, comparative form, verb form, adverb) and read the corrected sentence aloud. Brief explanation of the rule for each error.
Students write one sentence of their own that contains a deliberate error, then swap with a partner to spot and correct it. This consolidates the error-recognition skill in an active, playful way.

periods.teacher_notes: The ten sentences cover several grammar concepts — subject-verb agreement, comparative adjectives, adverbs of manner, and verb tense. Sentences 1–5 are tackled in class; sentences 6–10 are set for home practice to allow depth over breadth. Students often confuse 'taller than' with 'tall than' — worth calling out specifically during the class review.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — C. (p.111): observe labelled tool pictures and discuss their uses and vocations.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws three simple tool outlines on the board — a hammer, a stethoscope, a sickle — and asks students to name each and say who uses it. This warm-up links tools to professions before the fuller set is encountered.

Let us Learn — C. (p.111): Students open textbooks to the picture set (telescope, hammer, camera, screwdriver, sickle, stethoscope, grater, tongs, compass, mouse, saw). In pairs, students say the name of each tool, whether they have seen it, and what it is used for. Teacher circulates and prompts with 'Which job uses this?'

Whole-class share: teacher points to each picture in turn; students name the tool and the vocation it belongs to. Teacher adds any profession names students do not know. Class builds a two-column board list: tool — vocation.
Students choose any two tools from the picture set and write one sentence about each, saying what job requires that tool and why. Sentences are shared aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: This vocabulary task extends the poem's theme of vocations into the wider world of tools and professions. 'Compass' and 'mouse' may prompt discussion of different meanings (navigational compass vs. drawing compass; computer mouse vs. animal) — these are welcome teaching moments about polysemy. Link back to the poem's spade and lantern as the tools of the gardener and watchman.

periods.activity_title: Planning and Writing — The Hidden Hardships

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — 1. (p.114): plan and draft paragraph on the difficult side of a worker's job.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recalls the poem's three workers aloud and asks: 'The child sees only the fun part. What might be hard or boring?' Whole class brainstorms; teacher notes ideas on the board in rough columns: hawker / gardener / watchman.

Let us Write — 1. (p.114): Teacher models writing a short paragraph on one worker — thinking aloud the planning steps: choose a worker, name two hardships, explain with a detail, close with a concluding thought. Students watch and listen, then copy the plan frame into their notebooks.

Let us Write — 1. (p.114): Students choose one of the three workers and write their own paragraph using the plan frame. Teacher circulates and gives brief formative feedback — checking that the student has named a specific hardship and used at least one detail from the poem's description of that worker.
Three or four students volunteer to read their paragraphs aloud. Class listens and offers one compliment and one question each. Teacher collects notebooks to provide written feedback.

periods.teacher_notes: The modelled paragraph is crucial — students at this stage benefit from seeing the planning frame before they write independently. A common pitfall is writing that the hawker 'gets tired', without any specific detail; nudge students toward concrete imaginings like walking in heat, carrying heavy bags, or being ignored by passersby — details the poem's imagery can inspire. Drafting, peer response, and revision are all contained within this sitting.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — 2. (p.114): write about the vocations of three family members (50–60 words each).

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the task instructions aloud and asks students to think silently: which three family members will they write about, and what does each one do? Students jot two or three words for each person in a rough plan.

Let us Write — 2. (p.114): Students write about three family members, one at a time, in their notebooks. Each piece should say what the person does, describe one main daily task, and say why it matters. Teacher circulates, prompting students who have written fewer than three sentences to add a specific detail.

Students read back what they have written and check: Does each piece name the person and their job? Does it include one concrete detail? Students revise one sentence in each piece based on their own check.
Two volunteers share one of their three pieces aloud. Class listens; teacher notes one language strength from each reading for the class to hear.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often write very similar sentences for each family member — watch for this and prompt them to think about what is distinctive about each job. The 50–60 word guidance in the textbook keeps the task focused; students who write very short pieces should be nudged to add a specific daily activity. All three pieces are drafted, checked, and read within this single sitting.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — 3. (p.114): identify vocations of five famous Indians and write short answers.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the five names on the board — A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, M. Visvesvaraya, Janaki Ammal, M.S. Subbulakshmi, Salim Ali — and asks students if they recognise any. Students share what they know; teacher fills gaps with a sentence about each person's field.

Let us Write — 3. (p.114): Students write a short answer for each name, identifying the vocation and a brief reason (one or two supporting facts they heard in the opening discussion or already know). Teacher circulates, ensuring students name the specific field — scientist, engineer, botanist, musician, ornithologist — not just 'a famous person'.
Class review: teacher takes each name in turn; students read their answers aloud and refine wording together. Teacher writes the agreed vocation label beside each name on the board.
Brief discussion: the poem is about workers the child sees on the street; Tagore himself was a poet — what would the poem's child have thought of Tagore's vocation? Students share a thought or two.

periods.teacher_notes: Some students may know Abdul Kalam as a former President rather than as a scientist — it is worth noting both roles and letting them see that a person's vocation and their office can differ. Janaki Ammal and Salim Ali are less well known at this grade; the brief teacher introduction in the opening band is important. The closing discussion links the writing task back to the poem's broader theme.

periods.activity_title: Job Mix-Up and Dream Vocation — Beyond the Poem

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do (p.115): observe Job Mix-Up pictures and write two sentences per picture.
Let us Explore — A, B, C (pp.116–118): choose a dream vocation, discuss reasons, and draw self in that role.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do (p.115): Students open textbooks to the Job Mix-Up pictures. In pairs, students observe each picture, name what is unusual, and write two sentences per picture in their notebooks following the model provided. Teacher circulates, checking that sentences name the correct job for the professional shown.

Let us Explore — A and B (pp.116–117): Teacher walks students through the eight vocation illustrations. Students study them briefly, then discuss with a partner: which vocation would you choose, and is there a dream job not shown? Each student shares one choice and one reason with the class.

Let us Explore — C (p.118): Students draw themselves in their chosen vocation in the blank space provided in the textbook (or in their notebooks). They add a caption naming the vocation and one tool or action that belongs to it.

Quick gallery moment: students hold up or display their drawings. Teacher invites three or four students to say their vocation name and caption aloud. The chapter closes with the class having named and claimed a vocation of their own — the poem's child wished; these students chose.

periods.teacher_notes: The Job Mix-Up pictures give students a playful, image-led start before the more reflective Explore discussion. Encourage students to name the correct professional in their Job Mix-Up sentences (e.g. 'The chef should be cooking, not driving a fire engine') rather than just describing what they see. The drawing and caption in the final activity bring the chapter's central theme — vocation as identity and aspiration — to a personal close.

items.item_stem: In the poem, the child speaker watches three different workers during the day. Which of the following correctly matches the time of day with the worker the speaker notices?

options.label: A
options.text: Morning — gardener; Afternoon — watchman; Evening — hawker

options.label: B
options.text: Morning — hawker; Afternoon — gardener; Evening — watchman

options.label: C
options.text: Morning — hawker; Afternoon — watchman; Evening — gardener

options.label: D
options.text: Morning — watchman; Afternoon — hawker; Evening — gardener

what_each_option_reveals.A: Students choosing this have mixed up the sequence of the three stanzas.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Students choosing this may remember the watchman vividly but have misplaced him at the start of the day.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Students choosing this have correctly placed the hawker in the morning but confused the afternoon and evening workers.

items.item_stem: In the third stanza of the poem, the speaker describes the street-lamp in a striking way. Read the lines on page 106 beginning "The lane is dark and lonely" and explain: what does the street-lamp look like to the speaker, and why do you think the poet chose that particular image?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The speaker compares the street-lamp to a giant with one red eye in its head. The poet likely chose this image because it makes the lonely, dark lane feel both mysterious and slightly frightening — exactly the kind of scene that would appeal to a child's imagination.

items.source_context: Speaker's admiration of three workers' freedom; WH-question creation; personal narrative of wanting to do many things.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the following two statements and decide whether each is true or false. Be ready to say one reason for your answer.
1. The speaker in the poem admires the hawker because hawkers earn a great deal of money.
2. The speaker admires the gardener because the gardener can work freely without anyone scolding him.

options.text: The speaker admires the gardener because the gardener can work freely without anyone scolding him.
The speaker in the poem admires the hawker because hawkers earn a great deal of money.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statement 1 is false: the speaker admires the hawker for his freedom to wander with no fixed road or time, not for wealth. Statement 2 is true: the poem says nobody takes the gardener to task, meaning he faces no reprimand for getting dirty or staying in the sun.

items.item_stem: The poem's speaker describes a time every day when he wishes he could be someone else. Think of a real moment when you wanted to do something freely but something stopped you. Tell your class: what did you want to do, what stopped you, and how did it feel?

expected_elements: Names a specific activity they wanted to do.
Expresses the feeling in their own words.

items.item_stem: The poem's speaker says the watchman never goes to bed in his life. Write one sentence that correctly describes what the watchman actually does at night, as the poem tells us.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The watchman walks up and down the dark and lonely lane all night, swinging his lantern with his shadow at his side.

items.item_stem: The poem's child notices only the exciting side of the hawker's life — shouting out his wares and walking freely. Write a short paragraph (3–4 sentences) imagining one difficult or tiring part of being a hawker that the child does not think about.

expected_elements: Names a specific hardship linked to the hawker's job.
Uses at least one concrete detail (heat, weight, no customers).
Shows understanding that real work involves difficulty.

Describes at least one daily task in that job.
